name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q01 - Reaction of concentrated sulphuric acid with halides

questiontext.text: On addition of conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) to a chloride salt, colourless fumes are evolved but in case of iodide salt, violet fumes come out. This is because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Concentrated sulphuric acid (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\)) acts both as a strong acid and as a moderately strong oxidising agent. The reducing power of hydrogen halides (\(\mathrm{HX}\)) increases down the group in the order \(\mathrm{HF} < \mathrm{HCl} < \mathrm{HBr} < \mathrm{HI}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
When conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) is added to a chloride salt, \(\mathrm{HCl}\) gas is evolved as colourless fumes. Because \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is a weak reducing agent, it is not oxidised by conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\).

Step 3: Application
When conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) is added to an iodide salt, \(\mathrm{HI}\) is initially formed. However, \(\mathrm{HI}\) is a strong reducing agent and immediately reduces \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) to \(\mathrm{SO}_2\), while \(\mathrm{HI}\) itself gets oxidised to \(\mathrm{I}_2\), which evolves as violet fumes:
\(2\mathrm{HI} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \rightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + \mathrm{SO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Violet fumes appear because \(\mathrm{HI}\) gets oxidised to \(\mathrm{I}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q02 - Qualitative analysis of copper sulphide with ammonia

questiontext.text: In qualitative analysis when \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) is passed through an aqueous solution of salt acidified with dil. \(\mathrm{HCl}\), a black precipitate is obtained. On boiling the precipitate with dil. \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\), it forms a solution of blue colour. Addition of excess of aqueous solution of ammonia to this solution gives

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Group II qualitative analysis, passing \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\) through an acidified solution precipitates \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions as black copper(II) sulphide (\(\mathrm{CuS}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
On boiling the black \(\mathrm{CuS}\) precipitate with dilute \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\), it dissolves to form a blue aqueous solution of copper(II) nitrate, \(\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2}\):
\(3\mathrm{CuS} + 8\mathrm{HNO}_3 \rightarrow 3\mathrm{Cu(NO_3)_2} + 2\mathrm{NO} + 3\mathrm{S} + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

Step 3: Application
When excess aqueous ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)) is added to the blue solution containing \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) ions, a soluble, intensely coloured tetraamminecopper(II) complex ion is formed:
\(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \left[\mathrm{Cu(NH_3)_4}\right]^{2+}(\mathrm{aq})\)

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Addition of excess aqueous ammonia produces a deep blue solution of \(\left[\mathrm{Cu}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{4}\right]^{2+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q03 - Single and double bonds in cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid

questiontext.text: In a cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid molecule, how many single and double bonds are present?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The molecule is cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid, which has the molecular formula \((\mathrm{HPO}_3)_3\) or \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{P}_3\mathrm{O}_9\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Each phosphorus atom is pentavalent (forms 5 covalent bonds), oxygen is divalent, and hydrogen is monovalent.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid has a six-membered cyclic ring consisting of three alternating phosphorus atoms and three oxygen atoms connected by \(\mathrm{P-O-P}\) linkages. Each phosphorus atom is also bonded to one oxo group (\(=\mathrm{O}\)) and one hydroxyl group (\(-\mathrm{OH}\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Count the double bonds:
Each of the 3 phosphorus atoms has one \(\mathrm{P=O}\) double bond, giving \(3\) double bonds.
Count the single bonds:
1. Ring \(\mathrm{P-O}\) single bonds: \(6\) single bonds (two per \(\mathrm{P}\) atom in the 6-membered ring).
2. Exocyclic \(\mathrm{P-O}\) single bonds to the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups: \(3\) single bonds (one per \(\mathrm{P}\) atom).
3. \(\mathrm{O-H}\) single bonds in the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups: \(3\) single bonds.
Total single bonds \(= 6 + 3 + 3 = 12\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Total valence bonds: \(3\) double bonds and \(12\) single bonds. Thus, cyclotrimetaphosphoric acid contains 3 double bonds and 12 single bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q04 - Element capable of p-pi d-pi bonding

questiontext.text: Which of the following elements can be involved in \(\mathrm{p}\pi\text{–}\mathrm{d}\pi\) bonding?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For an element to participate in \(\mathrm{p}\pi\text{–}\mathrm{d}\pi\) bonding, it must possess vacant \(d\)-orbitals of suitable energy in its valence shell.

Step 2: Evaluation
Boron (\(\mathrm{B}\)), carbon (\(\mathrm{C}\)), and nitrogen (\(\mathrm{N}\)) belong to the second period of the periodic table. Their valence shell is \(n = 2\), which contains only \(2s\) and \(2p\) orbitals and lacks \(d\)-orbitals.

Step 3: Application
Phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}\)) belongs to the third period (\(n = 3\)), so it has vacant \(3d\) orbitals available in its valence shell. Therefore, phosphorus can form \(\mathrm{p}\pi\text{–}\mathrm{d}\pi\) bonds (for example, with oxygen in \(\mathrm{PO}_4^{3-}\) or \(\mathrm{P}_4\mathrm{O}_{10}\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Phosphorus can be involved in \(\mathrm{p}\pi\text{–}\mathrm{d}\pi\) bonding.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q05 - Isoelectronic and isostructural ion pairs

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs of ions are isoelectronic and isostructural?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The ions to be compared are \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\), \(\mathrm{NO}_3^{-}\), \(\mathrm{ClO}_3^{-}\), and \(\mathrm{SO}_3^{2-}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Isoelectronic species have the same total number of electrons (or valence electrons). Isostructural species have the same hybridisation on the central atom and the same molecular geometry.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total electrons \(=\) sum of atomic numbers of all atoms \(+\) negative charge. Geometry is determined by VSEPR theory via steric number \(=\frac{1}{2}(V + M - C + A)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\):
Total electrons \(= 6 + 3(8) + 2 = 32\).
Central carbon atom has \(3\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs (\(sp^2\) hybridised), giving a trigonal planar geometry.
For \(\mathrm{NO}_3^{-}\):
Total electrons \(= 7 + 3(8) + 1 = 32\).
Central nitrogen atom has \(3\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs (\(sp^2\) hybridised), giving a trigonal planar geometry.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\) and \(\mathrm{NO}_3^{-}\) have \(32\) electrons and trigonal planar structure, so they are isoelectronic and isostructural.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q06 - Bond dissociation enthalpy of halogen acids

questiontext.text: Affinity for hydrogen decreases in the group from fluorine to iodine. Which of the halogen acids should have highest bond dissociation enthalpy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bond dissociation enthalpy of a covalent \(\mathrm{H-X}\) bond depends inversely on the bond length and directly on the extent of orbital overlap between hydrogen and the halogen atom.

Step 2: Evaluation
Moving down Group 17 from fluorine to iodine, the atomic size of the halogen increases. Consequently, the \(\mathrm{H-X}\) bond length increases in the order \(\mathrm{H-F} < \mathrm{H-Cl} < \mathrm{H-Br} < \mathrm{H-I}\).

Step 3: Application
Since fluorine is the smallest halogen, the \(1s\text{–}2p\) orbital overlap in \(\mathrm{HF}\) is the strongest and the \(\mathrm{H-F}\) bond is the shortest, requiring the maximum energy to break.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{HF}\) has the highest bond dissociation enthalpy among the halogen acids.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q07 - Reducing strength of group 15 hydrides

questiontext.text:
Bond dissociation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) (\(\mathrm{E} = \text{element}\)) bonds is given below. Which of the compounds will act as strongest reducing agent?

Compound\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)\(\mathrm{AsH}_3\)\(\mathrm{SbH}_3\)
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{diss}}(\mathrm{E\text{—}H})/\mathrm{kJ\,mol}^{-1}\)389322297255

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) bond dissociation enthalpies are: \(\mathrm{NH}_3 = 389\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{PH}_3 = 322\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{AsH}_3 = 297\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), and \(\mathrm{SbH}_3 = 255\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A hydride acts as a reducing agent by donating hydrogen atoms (or electrons) upon cleavage of the \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) bond.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Reducing character of hydrides is inversely proportional to the \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) bond dissociation enthalpy: the weaker the \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) bond, the more readily hydrogen is released, and the stronger the reducing agent.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Comparing the given values:
\(389 > 322 > 297 > 255\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\mathrm{SbH}_3\) has the lowest \(\mathrm{E\text{—}H}\) bond dissociation enthalpy (\(255\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) because \(\mathrm{Sb}\) has the largest atomic size among the listed Group 15 elements, leading to the longest and weakest \(\mathrm{Sb\text{—}H}\) bond.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(\mathrm{SbH}_3\) loses hydrogen most easily, \(\mathrm{SbH}_3\) acts as the strongest reducing agent.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q08 - Properties of phosphine gas from white phosphorus

questiontext.text: On heating with concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution in an inert atmosphere of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\), white phosphorus gives a gas. Which of the following statement is incorrect about the gas?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
White phosphorus reacts with concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution in an inert atmosphere of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) to produce phosphine gas (\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)):
\(\mathrm{P}_4 + 3\mathrm{NaOH} + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{PH}_3 + 3\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\)

Step 2: Evaluation
Phosphine (\(\mathrm{PH}_3\)) is a colourless, highly poisonous gas with a rotten fish smell, and its aqueous solution decomposes in the presence of light to give red phosphorus and \(\mathrm{H}_2\).

Step 3: Application
Comparing basicity, phosphorus is larger and less electronegative than nitrogen, and the lone pair on phosphorus in \(\mathrm{PH}_3\) resides in a more diffused \(s\)-rich orbital compared to the \(sp^3\) orbital in \(\mathrm{NH}_3\). Therefore, \(\mathrm{PH}_3\) is a much weaker base than \(\mathrm{NH}_3\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The statement that the gas is more basic than \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) is incorrect.

answer.text: It is highly poisonous and has smell like rotten fish.
Its solution in water decomposes in the presence of light.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q09 - Tribasic acid forming three series of salts

questiontext.text: Which of the following acids forms three series of salts?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The number of series of salts formed by an acid corresponds to its basicity, which for oxoacids of phosphorus equals the number of ionisable \(\mathrm{P-OH}\) groups.

Step 2: Evaluation
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) has one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group and two \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds, so it is monobasic (1 series of salts).
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{BO}_3\) is a weak monobasic Lewis acid (accepts one \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ion).
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3\) has two \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups and one \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bond, so it is dibasic (2 series of salts).
- \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) (orthophosphoric acid) has three \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups attached to phosphorus and is tribasic.

Step 3: Application
Because \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) has three ionisable protons, it forms three series of salts: \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_4\), \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{HPO}_4\), and \(\mathrm{Na}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\) forms three series of salts.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q10 - Cause of strong reducing behaviour of hypophosphorous acid

questiontext.text: Strong reducing behaviour of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) is due to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In oxoacids of phosphorus, the reducing property is governed by the presence of \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds directly attached to the phosphorus atom.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hypophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\), phosphinic acid) has a tetrahedral phosphorus centre bonded to one \(=\mathrm{O}\) atom, one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group, and two \(\mathrm{H}\) atoms.

Step 3: Application
The two \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds can be readily oxidised to \(\mathrm{P-OH}\) bonds, making \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) a strong reducing agent (for example, reducing \(\mathrm{AgNO}_3\) to metallic \(\mathrm{Ag}\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The strong reducing behaviour of \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_2\) is due to the presence of one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group and two \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds.

answer.text: Presence of two \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups and one \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bond
Presence of one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group and two \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q11 - Thermal decomposition products of lead nitrate

questiontext.text: On heating lead nitrate forms oxides of nitrogen and lead. The oxides formed are

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Heavy metal nitrates decompose upon heating to give the metal oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide gas (\(\mathrm{NO}_2\)), and oxygen gas (\(\mathrm{O}_2\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
Lead(II) nitrate undergoes thermal decomposition according to the balanced equation:
\(2\mathrm{Pb(NO_3)_2(s)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\mathrm{PbO(s)} + 4\mathrm{NO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + \mathrm{O}_2\mathrm{(g)}\)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The oxides formed are \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{PbO}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q12 - Allotropy in group 15 elements

questiontext.text: Which of the following elements does not show allotropy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Allotropy in Group 15 elements depends on the ability of the element to form catenated or polymeric single-bonded structures.

Step 2: Evaluation
Phosphorus, arsenic, antimony, and bismuth exhibit allotropy. Nitrogen, however, has a very small atomic size, which leads to high interelectronic repulsion between non-bonding lone pairs on adjacent nitrogen atoms in a single \(\mathrm{N-N}\) bond.

Step 3: Application
Because the \(\mathrm{N-N}\) single bond is very weak compared to the \(\mathrm{N\equiv N}\) triple bond, nitrogen exists exclusively as discrete diatomic \(\mathrm{N}_2\) molecules and does not form polymeric allotropes.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Nitrogen does not show allotropy.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q13 - Maximum covalency of nitrogen

questiontext.text: Maximum covalency of nitrogen is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The maximum covalency of an element is limited by the total number of orbitals available in its valence shell for bonding.

Step 2: Evaluation
Nitrogen has the ground-state valence electronic configuration \(2s^2 2p^3\). Its valence shell (\(n = 2\)) has only one \(2s\) orbital and three \(2p\) orbitals, and no \(2d\) orbitals exist.

Step 3: Application
With four valence orbitals in total, nitrogen can form a maximum of four covalent bonds (for example, in \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\) or \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5\)), which restricts its maximum covalency to 4.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The maximum covalency of nitrogen is 4.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q14 - Incorrect statement about nitrogen and phosphorus compounds

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is wrong?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bond strength of single homonuclear bonds in second-period elements with lone pairs is weakened by interelectronic repulsion between lone pairs on adjacent small atoms.

Step 2: Evaluation
- In a single \(\mathrm{N-N}\) bond, the small size of nitrogen atoms causes strong lone-pair–lone-pair repulsion, making the \(\mathrm{N-N}\) single bond weaker than the \(\mathrm{P-P}\) single bond.
- \(\mathrm{PH}_3\) has a lone pair of electrons on phosphorus and can act as a ligand with transition metals.
- \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) has an odd number of electrons (one unpaired electron), making it paramagnetic.
- In \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_5\), each nitrogen atom forms four covalent bonds (covalency is 4).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement that a single \(\mathrm{N-N}\) bond is stronger than a single \(\mathrm{P-P}\) bond is wrong.

answer.text: Single \(\mathrm{N-N}\) bond is stronger than the single \(\mathrm{P-P}\) bond.
\(\mathrm{PH}_3\) can act as a ligand in the formation of coordination compound with transition elements.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q15 - Brown ring test complex for nitrate ion

questiontext.text: A brown ring is formed in the ring test for \(\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) ion. It is due to the formation of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the brown ring test for nitrate ions (\(\mathrm{NO}_3^-\)), freshly prepared \(\mathrm{FeSO}_4\) solution reduces \(\mathrm{NO}_3^-\) to nitric oxide (\(\mathrm{NO}\)) in the presence of concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The reactions involved are:
\(\mathrm{NO}_3^- + 3\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} + 4\mathrm{H}^+ \rightarrow \mathrm{NO} + 3\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)
\(\left[\mathrm{Fe(H_2O)_6}\right]^{2+} + \mathrm{NO} \rightarrow \left[\mathrm{Fe(H_2O)_5(NO)}\right]^{2+} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The brown ring is due to the formation of the complex \(\left[\mathrm{Fe}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\right)_{5}(\mathrm{NO})\right]^{2+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q16 - Well characterised bismuth compound in +5 oxidation state

questiontext.text: Elements of group-15 form compounds in \(+5\) oxidation state. However, bismuth forms only one well characterised compound in \(+5\) oxidation state. The compound is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Due to the inert pair effect, the stability of the \(+5\) oxidation state decreases down Group 15, while the \(+3\) oxidation state becomes progressively more stable. Thus, \(\mathrm{Bi(V)}\) is a very strong oxidising agent.

Step 2: Evaluation
Only the most electronegative and smallest halogen, fluorine, can stabilise bismuth in its \(+5\) oxidation state by forming \(\mathrm{BiF}_5\). Less electronegative elements like chlorine, oxygen, or sulphur are oxidised by \(\mathrm{Bi(V)}\) and cannot form stable, well-characterised \(\mathrm{Bi(V)}\) compounds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The only well-characterised compound of bismuth in the \(+5\) oxidation state is \(\mathrm{BiF}_5\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q17 - Thermal decomposition of ammonium dichromate and barium azide

questiontext.text: On heating ammonium dichromate and barium azide separately we get

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both ammonium dichromate and metal azides undergo thermal decomposition to liberate dinitrogen (\(\mathrm{N}_2\)) gas.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. Thermal decomposition of ammonium dichromate:
\((\mathrm{NH}_4)_2\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{N}_2 + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)
2. Thermal decomposition of barium azide (gives very pure \(\mathrm{N}_2\)):
\(\mathrm{Ba(N_3)_2} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{Ba} + 3\mathrm{N}_2\)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Heating ammonium dichromate and barium azide separately yields \(\mathrm{N}_2\) in both cases.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{N}_2\) with ammonium dichromate and \(\mathrm{NO}\) with barium azide
\(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}\) with ammonium dichromate and \(\mathrm{N}_2\) with barium azide
\(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}\) with ammonium dichromate and \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) with barium azide

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q18 - Stoichiometry of catalytic oxidation of ammonia

questiontext.text: In the preparation of \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\), we get \(\mathrm{NO}\) gas by catalytic oxidation of ammonia. The moles of \(\mathrm{NO}\) produced by the oxidation of two moles of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) will be ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Moles of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) oxidised \(= 2\text{ mol}\). Process: catalytic oxidation of ammonia in Ostwald's process for \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) preparation.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Oxygen is present in excess so that ammonia undergoes complete catalytic oxidation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The balanced chemical equation for the catalytic oxidation of ammonia over a \(\mathrm{Pt/Rh}\) gauze catalyst at \(500\text{ K}\) and \(9\text{ bar}\) is:
\(4\mathrm{NH}_3\mathrm{(g)} + 5\mathrm{O}_2\mathrm{(g)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pt/Rh},\,500\text{ K},\,9\text{ bar}} 4\mathrm{NO(g)} + 6\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(g)}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
From the stoichiometry of the balanced equation, \(4\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) produce \(4\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NO}\).
Therefore, the molar ratio \(\mathrm{NH}_3 : \mathrm{NO} = 1 : 1\).
For \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\):
\(\text{Moles of NO} = 2\text{ mol}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Nitrogen atoms are conserved (\(2\text{ mol N}\) in \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) gives \(2\text{ mol N}\) in \(\mathrm{NO}\)). Thus, 2 moles of \(\mathrm{NO}\) are produced.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q19 - Oxidation state of phosphorus in sodium hypophosphite

questiontext.text: The oxidation state of central atom in the anion of compound \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\) will be ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The compound is \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\). Its anion is \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{PO}_2^-\), with central atom phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard oxidation numbers: \(\mathrm{H} = +1\) and \(\mathrm{O} = -2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The algebraic sum of oxidation numbers of all atoms in a polyatomic ion equals the net charge on the ion.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Let the oxidation state of \(\mathrm{P}\) in \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{PO}_2^-\) be \(x\).
\(2(+1) + x + 2(-2) = -1\)
\(2 + x - 4 = -1\)
\(x - 2 = -1\)
\(x = +1\)

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking with the neutral salt \(\mathrm{NaH}_2\mathrm{PO}_2\): \(+1 + 2(+1) + (+1) + 2(-2) = 0\). Thus, the oxidation state of phosphorus is \(+1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q20 - Identifying non-tetrahedral species

questiontext.text: Which of the following is not tetrahedral in shape?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Molecular shape is determined by the number of bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom according to VSEPR theory.

Step 2: Evaluation
- \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\): Central \(\mathrm{N}\) has \(4\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs (\(sp^3\)) \(\rightarrow\) tetrahedral.
- \(\mathrm{SiCl}_4\): Central \(\mathrm{Si}\) has \(4\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs (\(sp^3\)) \(\rightarrow\) tetrahedral.
- \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\): Central \(\mathrm{S}\) has \(4\) \(\sigma\)-bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs (\(sp^3\)) \(\rightarrow\) tetrahedral.
- \(\mathrm{SF}_4\): Central \(\mathrm{S}\) has \(6\) valence electrons; \(4\) are used in forming \(\mathrm{S-F}\) bonds and \(2\) remain as \(1\) lone pair. This gives a steric number of \(5\) (\(sp^3d\) hybridisation, trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry).

Step 3: Application
With \(4\) bond pairs and \(1\) lone pair in an equatorial position, \(\mathrm{SF}_4\) adopts a see-saw shape rather than a tetrahedral shape.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{SF}_4\) is not tetrahedral in shape.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q21 - Identifying peroxoacids of sulphur

questiontext.text: Which of the following are peroxoacids of sulphur?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Peroxoacids of sulphur are oxoacids that contain at least one peroxo linkage (\(\mathrm{-O-O-}\)) in their structure.

Step 2: Evaluation
- \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_5\) (peroxomonosulphuric acid, Caro's acid) contains one \(\mathrm{-O-O-}\) linkage.
- \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_8\) (peroxodisulphuric acid, Marshall's acid) contains one \(\mathrm{-O-O-}\) linkage between the two sulphur-centred tetrahedral units.
- \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_7\) (pyrosulphuric acid or oleum) contains a \(\mathrm{S-O-S}\) oxide bridge, not a peroxo linkage.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_5\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}_2\mathrm{O}_8\) are peroxoacids of sulphur.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q22 - Oxidation of carbon by hot concentrated sulphuric acid

questiontext.text: Hot conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) acts as moderately strong oxidising agent. It oxidises both metals and nonmetals. Which of the following element is oxidised by conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) into two gaseous products?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hot concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) oxidises metals and non-metals while itself being reduced to \(\mathrm{SO}_2\) gas.

Step 2: Evaluation
- Copper: \(\mathrm{Cu} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4(\text{conc.}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO}_4 + \mathrm{SO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (only one gaseous product, \(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).
- Sulphur: \(\mathrm{S} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4(\text{conc.}) \rightarrow 3\mathrm{SO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (only one gaseous product, \(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).
- Zinc: \(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4(\text{conc.}) \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO}_4 + \mathrm{SO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (only one gaseous product, \(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).
- Carbon: \(\mathrm{C} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4(\text{conc.}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + 2\mathrm{SO}_2\mathrm{(g)} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) (two gaseous products, \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Carbon (\(\mathrm{C}\)) is oxidised by hot conc. \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) into two gaseous products (\(\mathrm{CO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{SO}_2\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q23 - Oxidation state change of nitrogen in reaction with excess chlorine

questiontext.text: A black compound of manganese reacts with a halogen acid to give greenish yellow gas. When excess of this gas reacts with \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) an unstable trihalide is formed. In this process the oxidation state of nitrogen changes from

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Manganese dioxide (\(\mathrm{MnO}_2\), a black compound) oxidises concentrated hydrochloric acid (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)) to liberate greenish-yellow chlorine gas (\(\mathrm{Cl}_2\)):
\(\mathrm{MnO}_2 + 4\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnCl}_2 + \mathrm{Cl}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

Step 2: Evaluation
When excess \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\) reacts with \(\mathrm{NH}_3\), it forms the explosive, unstable nitrogen trichloride (\(\mathrm{NCl}_3\)):
\(\mathrm{NH}_3 + 3\mathrm{Cl}_2\text{ (excess)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NCl}_3 + 3\mathrm{HCl}\)

Step 3: Application
In \(\mathrm{NH}_3\), hydrogen has oxidation state \(+1\), so nitrogen has oxidation state \(-3\).
In \(\mathrm{NCl}_3\), chlorine is more electronegative than nitrogen and has oxidation state \(-1\), so nitrogen has oxidation state \(+3\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The oxidation state of nitrogen changes from \(-3\) to \(+3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q24 - Reason for Bartlett using O2+PtF6- for xenon compounds

questiontext.text: In the preparation of compounds of \(\mathrm{Xe}\), Bartlett had taken \(\mathrm{O}_2^+\,\mathrm{PtF}_6^-\) as a base compound. This is because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Neil Bartlett observed that \(\mathrm{PtF}_6\) oxidised molecular oxygen (\(\mathrm{O}_2\)) to form the ionic compound \(\mathrm{O}_2^+\mathrm{PtF}_6^-\).

Step 2: Evaluation
He noticed that the first ionisation enthalpy of molecular oxygen (\(1175\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) is almost identical to the first ionisation enthalpy of xenon (\(1170\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)).

Step 3: Application
Reasoning that \(\mathrm{PtF}_6\) should similarly be able to oxidise xenon, Bartlett reacted \(\mathrm{Xe}\) with \(\mathrm{PtF}_6\) and prepared the first noble gas compound, \(\mathrm{Xe}^+\mathrm{PtF}_6^-\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both \(\mathrm{O}_2\) and \(\mathrm{Xe}\) have almost the same ionisation enthalpy.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q25 - Structure of phosphorus pentachloride in solid state

questiontext.text: In solid state \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) is a

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
While \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) exists as discrete trigonal bipyramidal molecules in the gaseous and liquid phases, it undergoes autoionisation in the solid state to achieve greater lattice stability.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the solid state, \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) exists as an ionic solid composed of \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_4\right]^+\) cations and \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_6\right]^-\) anions.

Step 3: Application
- In \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_4\right]^+\), phosphorus is \(sp^3\) hybridised with \(4\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs, giving a tetrahedral geometry.
- In \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_6\right]^-\), phosphorus is \(sp^3d^2\) hybridised with \(6\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs, giving an octahedral geometry.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
In the solid state, \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) is an ionic solid with \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_4\right]^+\) tetrahedral and \(\left[\mathrm{PCl}_6\right]^-\) octahedral.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q26 - Decreasing order of oxidising power from reduction potentials

questiontext.text:
Reduction potentials of some ions are given below. Arrange them in decreasing order of oxidising power.

Ion\(\mathrm{ClO}_4^-\)\(\mathrm{IO}_4^-\)\(\mathrm{BrO}_4^-\)
Reduction potential \(E^\circ/\mathrm{V}\)\(E^\circ = 1.19\,\mathrm{V}\)\(E^\circ = 1.65\,\mathrm{V}\)\(E^\circ = 1.74\,\mathrm{V}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard reduction potentials (\(E^\circ\)):
\(E^\circ(\mathrm{ClO}_4^-) = 1.19\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ(\mathrm{IO}_4^-) = 1.65\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ(\mathrm{BrO}_4^-) = 1.74\text{ V}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Higher (more positive) standard reduction potential indicates a greater tendency for the species to gain electrons (be reduced).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Oxidising power is directly proportional to the standard reduction potential (\(E^\circ\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Arranging the \(E^\circ\) values in decreasing order:
\(1.74\text{ V} > 1.65\text{ V} > 1.19\text{ V}\).
Correspondingly, the decreasing order of oxidising power is:
\(\mathrm{BrO}_4^- > \mathrm{IO}_4^- > \mathrm{ClO}_4^-\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(\mathrm{BrO}_4^-\) has the highest reduction potential and \(\mathrm{ClO}_4^-\) the lowest, so the decreasing order of oxidising power is \(\mathrm{BrO}_4^- > \mathrm{IO}_4^- > \mathrm{ClO}_4^-\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQI_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q27 - Identifying isoelectronic halogen and interhalogen species

questiontext.text: Which of the following is isoelectronic pair?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Atomic numbers: \(\mathrm{C} = 6\), \(\mathrm{N} = 7\), \(\mathrm{O} = 8\), \(\mathrm{F} = 9\), \(\mathrm{Cl} = 17\), \(\mathrm{Br} = 35\), \(\mathrm{I} = 53\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Isoelectronic species have the same total number of electrons.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Total electrons} = \sum Z_i - \text{charge}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- \(\mathrm{ICl}_2\) and \(\mathrm{ClO}_2\): \(53 + 2(17) = 87\) vs. \(17 + 2(8) = 33\) (not equal).
- \(\mathrm{BrO}_2^-\) and \(\mathrm{BrF}_2^+\):
\(\mathrm{BrO}_2^- = 35 + 2(8) + 1 = 52\) electrons.
\(\mathrm{BrF}_2^+ = 35 + 2(9) - 1 = 52\) electrons (equal).
- \(\mathrm{ClO}_2\) and \(\mathrm{BrF}\): \(17 + 2(8) = 33\) vs. \(35 + 9 = 44\) (not equal).
- \(\mathrm{CN}^-\) and \(\mathrm{O}_3\): \(6 + 7 + 1 = 14\) vs. \(3(8) = 24\) (not equal).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both \(\mathrm{BrO}_2^-\) and \(\mathrm{BrF}_2^+\) have \(52\) electrons (and \(20\) valence electrons), so \(\mathrm{BrO}_2^-, \mathrm{BrF}_2^+\) is an isoelectronic pair.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQII_THEPBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q28 - Disproportionation of chlorine in hot sodium hydroxide

questiontext.text: If chlorine gas is passed through hot \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution, two changes are observed in the oxidation number of chlorine during the reaction. These are ______ and ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When chlorine gas reacts with hot and concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution, it undergoes a disproportionation reaction, simultaneously getting reduced and oxidised.

Step 2: Evaluation
The balanced chemical equation is:
\(3\mathrm{Cl}_2 + 6\mathrm{NaOH}\text{ (hot, conc.)} \rightarrow 5\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{NaClO}_3 + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)

Step 3: Application
- In \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\), the oxidation state of chlorine is \(0\).
- In \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), the oxidation state of chlorine is \(-1\) (reduction: \(0\) to \(-1\)).
- In \(\mathrm{NaClO}_3\), let the oxidation state of \(\mathrm{Cl}\) be \(x\): \(+1 + x + 3(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +5\) (oxidation: \(0\) to \(+5\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The two changes observed in the oxidation number of chlorine are \(0\) to \(+5\) and \(0\) to \(-1\).
